stories.title: Cerium-quercetin nanoparticles: antioxidant properties and therapeutic performance in sepsis
stories.description: Sepsis is a life-threatening syndrome driven by dysregulated inflammation, excessive oxidative stress, and progressive organ injury, yet therapies that concurrently control these interconnected processes remain limited. Restoring redox homeostasis while suppressing NF-κB-mediated inflammatory activation and correcting macrophage dysfunction therefore represents a key therapeutic objective. However, conventional antioxidant and anti-inflammatory agents are often constrained by limited stability, bioavailability, nonspecific distribution, and insufficient coordination of redox and immune regulation. Here, cerium-quercetin nanoparticles (CQ NPs) were prepared by combining cerium species with quercetin. CQ NPs exhibited concentration-dependent scavenging of ·OH and O2·−, reduced intracellular ROS level and apoptosis, preserved mitochondrial membrane potential, increased Nrf2 and HO-1 expression, decreased p-p65/p65 and p-IκBα/IκBα ratios, and altered CD86/CD206 expression. In mice with CLP-induced sepsis, CQ NPs reduced circulating TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-1β, attenuated pulmonary histopathological injury, and were associated with improved survival. These findings suggest that CQ NPs exhibit antioxidant and inflammation-associated effects in experimental sepsis, warranting further investigation into their underlying mechanisms and therapeutic potential.

stories.title: Comets may have destroyed life's ingredients instead of delivering them to Earth
stories.description: A century-old theory about the origins of life on Earth may be wrong. New research from the University of Cambridge suggests that comets traveled too fast and struck at unfavorable angles for the fragile molecules needed for life to survive, making successful delivery extraordinarily unlikely. Surprisingly, Mars may have had a better chance of receiving these cosmic ingredients, although even there the odds were slim. The findings point toward asteroids or chemical processes on Earth as more plausible sources of life's building blocks.
